responses.question: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
responses.response: Red. Pressing red is a weakly dominant choice: if blue wins, everyone (including you) survives regardless of what you press; if red wins, only red pressers survive. So red never makes you worse off and sometimes makes you better off.

responses.question: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
responses.response:
Short answer recap: I’d press red. For purely self-interested, causal decision-making, red is a weakly dominant action: holding everyone else’s choices fixed, red never leaves you worse off and sometimes leaves you strictly better off.

Why red looks dominant
- Consider the three relevant states of the world, fixing everyone else’s buttons:
  1) Others have a red majority: If you press red, you live; if you press blue, you die. Red is strictly better.
  2) Others have a blue majority: Everyone lives regardless; red and blue are equal for you.
  3) Others are exactly tied and you’re pivotal: If you press red, only reds live (including you); if you press blue, everyone lives (including you). Either way, you live; red and blue are equal for you personally.
- Therefore, for every profile of others’ choices, pressing red is at least as good for your survival as pressing blue, and sometimes strictly better. So if your sole objective is your own survival, red is the rational pick.
- “But if everyone reasons that way, won’t we get lots of red and kill the blue minority?” Perhaps—but note that if everyone presses red, everyone survives anyway. So your adopting the red rule isn’t steering the world to a universally bad equilibrium; both all-red and all-blue yield universal survival.

Steelmanning the case for pressing blue
There are strong arguments for blue that don’t rely on naive wishful thinking.

1) Altruistic impact when pivotal
- The only case where your single choice affects anyone else’s fate is when others are exactly tied. In that branch:
  - Pressing red kills the blue half.
  - Pressing blue saves everyone.
- Your own survival is unchanged in that pivotal branch. So if you assign any positive value to other people’s lives, blue is strictly better there. In a world with billions of people, even a tiny chance of being pivotal multiplies into a large expected number of lives saved at essentially no personal cost in that branch.

2) Superrational/functional decision theory
- If many people reason like you, your choice is logically correlated with theirs. You aren’t just choosing a button; you’re choosing a policy that many similar agents will also implement.
- Adopting the “press blue” policy helps coordinate that whole like-minded cluster toward a blue majority, which yields the forgiving outcome where everyone survives (including dissenters). This can improve your own survival chances if that correlated bloc is influential, and it produces a better social outcome.
- In policy-selection terms: pick the policy whose general adoption you most prefer. “Press blue” steers correlated agents to the Pareto-superior, failure-tolerant equilibrium.

3) Robustness and minority protection
- Blue-majority is inclusive: everyone lives even if some people deviate.
- Red-majority is punitive: the minority dies. In real, noisy coordination problems we want norms that are fault-tolerant. Pushing toward blue as a shared convention reduces systemic risk and protects minorities under imperfect coordination.

4) Long-run virtue and precedent
- Being the kind of agent that picks the Pareto-superior coordination point (blue) pays dividends across many analogous games—enabling trust, cooperation, and better equilibria with other similarly modeled agents. Even if this instance is private, you’re shaping the policy your future self and your “algorithmic neighbors” will follow.

Bottom line
- If you’re a narrow causal decision theorist maximizing only your own survival in this one shot, press red: it weakly dominates blue for you.
- If you care about acausal coordination, protecting minorities under miscoordination, or the expected number of lives saved when you’re pivotal (and/or you give weight to others’ welfare), you have strong reasons to press blue.

responses.question: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
responses.response:
Short caveat: These are tendencies, not rules. Individuals vary a lot, and framing strongly shifts choices.

Who tends to press blue (everyone-lives-if-majority-blue)
- Prosocial social value orientation: People who, in lab games, try to maximize joint outcomes or equality. This is often ~50–60% of participants in Western samples.
- Superrational/FDT-style reasoners: Folks who think “pick the policy I want correlated agents to follow” (e.g., some in rationalist/EA circles). They see their choice as linked to others like them and aim to coordinate on the inclusive equilibrium.
- High generalized-trust populations: People who believe many others will also try to cooperate/coordinate, and who come from environments with strong cooperative norms and low zero-sum thinking.
- Impartial altruists and “universalize-the-rule” moral reasoners: Those inclined to ask “what if everyone did this?” and to choose the Pareto-superior convention.
- People sensitive to being pivotal for others: If made aware that, in tie cases, blue saves everyone at no personal cost, they shift toward blue.
- Communities with strong coordination ethos: Open-source collaborators, disaster-response teams, cooperative enterprises—groups used to norms that protect minorities and are fault-tolerant.

Who tends to press red (self-survival weakly dominant)
- Narrow self-interest maximizers / causal decision theorists: Those who evaluate only their own survival holding others’ choices fixed. Red never hurts them and sometimes helps.
- Competitive/individualistic social value orientation: People who, in social-dilemma studies, prioritize own payoff or relative advantage over joint outcomes.
- Low-trust or highly adversarial mindsets: People expecting others to “defect” or seeing coordination as unreliable will default to the dominant-action safeguard.
- Trained dominance-reasoners: Students steeped in standard game-theory/econ pedagogy emphasizing weak dominance and equilibrium selection; competitive gamers/poker players with “never be the sucker” heuristics.
- People averse to acausal/logical-correlation arguments: If they treat others’ choices as independent noise, blue has no upside for self-survival, so they pick red.

Movable middle (framing and expectations matter)
- Public pledges and visible coordination efforts push people blue; emphasizing “your choice can save many when pivotal” increases blue.
- Emphasizing dominance logic or highlighting the risk of a red-majority pushes people red.
- In surveys/experiments on one-shot social dilemmas, cooperation rates typically sit around 40–60%; you should expect blue rates in that ballpark, rising in high-trust, coordination-savvy subcultures and falling in competitive, low-trust ones.

Very rough empirical expectations if you polled distinct groups
- Traditional econ/game-theory classrooms: majority red (e.g., 60–80%).
- Rationalist/EA communities familiar with superrationality/FDT: majority blue (e.g., 60–90%).
- General population, neutral framing: mixed, perhaps 40–70% blue depending on trust, prosociality, and how “pivotal” is explained.

Again, these are directional predictions grounded in social-dilemma research (social value orientation, generalized trust) and decision-theory norms, not hard demographic rules.

responses.question: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?
responses.response:
Short answer: Not necessarily. It depends on their goals and on how they think their choice relates to others’ choices.

When blue is “irrational”
- If you use narrow, causal decision theory and care only about your own survival, red weakly dominates blue. Holding others’ choices fixed, red never leaves you worse off and sometimes saves you when blue would kill you. In that specific model, choosing blue is instrumentally irrational.

When blue is rational
- Other-regarding preferences. If you put any weight on other people’s lives, blue can be the better expected-choice. Your action only changes others’ fates when you’re pivotal (others are exactly tied). In that branch, pressing blue saves roughly half the world at no personal cost. With billions of people, the chance of being pivotal is tiny, but the stakes are huge. Rule-of-thumb: with n people, blue saves about 0.4·sqrt(n) lives in expectation relative to red when you’re indifferent about the majority’s color. For n ≈ 8 billion, that’s ~36,000 expected lives. So if you value each stranger’s life at more than about 1.4×10^-5 of your own, blue maximizes your expected utility even under ordinary causal reasoning. 
- Superrational/functional or evidential decision theories. If you think many people reason like you, your policy is correlated with theirs. Choosing “press blue” helps steer that whole correlated bloc toward a blue majority, which is strictly safer and more inclusive. Under these views, blue can be rational even for a purely self-interested agent.
- Rule-consequentialist/Kantian reasoning. If you pick the rule you’d want everyone like you to follow, “press blue” selects the Pareto-superior convention that saves everyone whenever it wins, and it protects minorities under miscoordination.

Bottom line
- Under selfish causal decision theory: blue is (weakly) dominated and thus irrational by that standard.
- Under altruistic preferences, acausal/correlated-reasoning models, or rule-based ethics: blue is straightforwardly rational—and often strongly so.
